title: Queues and deques
summary: First in, first out, a circular buffer that never shifts, and the double-ended deque.

steps.title: First in, first out
body: A **queue** is a line at a till: join at the back (`Enqueue`), leave from the front (`Dequeue`). Whoever waited longest goes next.
Step through and watch the queue: items leave from the opposite end to where they joined.

steps.explain: Each `Enqueue(Dequeue())` moves the front item to the back: `abc` becomes `bca`, then `cab`.

steps.title: The circular buffer
body: A queue in an array has a problem: dequeuing from index 0 would shift everything left, `O(n)`.

Instead, keep a `head` index and a `count`, and let the indexes **wrap around** with `%`. The back slot is `(head + count) % capacity`. Nothing ever shifts, so both ends are `O(1)`. `Queue<T>` works exactly like this.
Watch the trace: after two dequeues, the new items land in the slots at the **start** of the array.

steps.prompt: Run the circular buffer from the card. What is its **last** line of output?
steps.explain: `head` is 2, so the queue reads from index 2: 3, 4, 5, 6. The array itself shows `5,6` at the front because they wrapped around.
hints: After the dequeues, `head = 2` and `count = 1`. The next item goes to `(2 + 1) % 4 = 3`, then `(2 + 2) % 4 = 0`.

steps.explain: The front is always at `head`. Moving `head` forward with `% buf.Length` wraps it back to 0 at the end.

steps.title: Deques: both ends
body: A **deque** (double-ended queue, said "deck") lets you add and remove at **both** ends in `O(1)`. It can act as a stack *and* a queue.
In .NET, `LinkedList<T>` is a doubly linked list and makes a good deque:

steps.prompt: Match each structure to its rule.
pairs: add and remove at the same end
add at the back, remove at the front
add and remove at either end
a fixed array whose indexes wrap with %

steps.explain: The list grows to `3 4 5 6`, then `RemoveLast` drops the 6.

steps.title: Build a ring queue
prompt: Write a class `RingQueue` backed by a fixed-size array:
- `bool Enqueue(int value)`: adds at the back; returns `false` (and changes nothing) when full.
- `int Dequeue()`: removes from the front; throws `InvalidOperationException` when empty.
Use `head` and `count` with `%`. Do not shift items, and do not use `Queue<T>` or `List<T>`.
starter: public RingQueue(int capacity) { buf = new int[capacity]; }
public int Count { get; private set; }
public bool Enqueue(int value) { return false; }
solution: public RingQueue(int capacity) { buf = new int[capacity]; }
public int Count { get; private set; }
template: Dojo.Eq("Enqueue returns true when there is room", true, dojoQ.Enqueue(1));
Dojo.Eq("Enqueue returns false when full", false, dojoQ.Enqueue(4));
for (var dojoI = 0; dojoI < 10; dojoI++) { dojoR.Enqueue(dojoI); dojoOut.Add(dojoR.Dequeue()); }
Dojo.Eq("keeps working after many wraps", Enumerable.Range(0, 10).ToList(), dojoOut);

forbid.message: Does not use Queue<T> or List<T>

hints: The back slot is `(head + Count) % buf.Length`.
